bib.title: Don't Do RAG: When Cache-Augmented Generation is All You Need for Knowledge Tasks

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Don't Do RAG: When Cache-Augmented Generation is All You Need for Knowledge Tasks", Brian J Chan, Chao-Ting Chen, Jui-Hung Cheng (National Chengchi University), Hen-Hsen Huang (Academia Sinica). WWW Companion '25 (Sydney, Apr 28-May 2, 2025), ACM; arXiv 2412.15605v2 (23 Feb 2025). Short companion paper, not a full conference track paper.

COVERAGE: 27,459 of 27,459 chars read (all pages, including tables, limitations and references). Nothing skipped. The only extraction faults are fontTools warnings, which I filtered out.

CLAIMS (ranked)
- CAG (preload the whole corpus, precompute the KV cache, no retrieval at query time) scored the highest BERTScore in most cells of the RAG comparison, on small corpora.
  number: HotPotQA small CAG 0.7951 vs best sparse RAG 0.7676 (top-5) and best dense RAG 0.7582 (top-3). HotPotQA medium 0.7821 vs 0.7633 sparse (top-5). SQuAD small 0.7695 vs 0.7616 sparse (top-3). SQuAD large 0.7734 vs 0.7658 sparse (top-5).
  setup: Llama 3.1 8B for every system. Corpora of 21k to 85k tokens. Metric is BERTScore against gold answers. Baselines built with LlamaIndex: BM25 and OpenAI-index dense retrieval, top-k of 1, 3, 5 and 10. Single run, no variance reported.
  quote: "CAG consistently achieved the highest BERTScore in most cases, outperforming both sparse and dense RAG methods."
  where: Section 3.3, Table 2 (p.3)
- The CAG advantage shrinks as the corpus grows. On HotPotQA large, CAG is roughly tied with sparse RAG and does not win.
  number: HotPotQA large CAG 0.7407 vs sparse top-5 0.7535 and sparse top-3 0.7463. Small-corpus margin over the best sparse run was 0.0275 (0.7951 vs 0.7676).
  setup: HotPotQA large is 64 docs, 85k tokens, 1,344 QA pairs. The authors say "slightly" narrows. By Table 2, CAG is below sparse top-3 and top-5 here. The "CAG wins in most cases" claim does not hold in this cell.
  quote: "However, as the data size increases, the performance gap between CAG and RAG narrows slightly, aligning with prior findings that long-context LLMs may experience degradation when handling very long contexts [6]."
  where: Section 3.3; Table 2
- Latency: CAG removes retrieval time. It also cuts generation time sharply compared with ordinary in-context learning, where the reference text is re-encoded on every query.
  number: HotPotQA small: CAG generation 0.8512 s vs in-context learning 9.3197 s. Medium: 1.4078 s vs 26.3717 s. Large: 2.2631 s vs 92.0824 s. Dense RAG top-3 retrieval is about 0.41 to 0.48 s. Sparse retrieval is 0.0008 to 0.0012 s. Sparse RAG top-3 generation is about 0.67 to 0.74 s, which is faster than CAG. Dense top-10 generation is about 2.64 to 2.66 s.
  setup: Tesla V100 32G x 8, Llama 3.1 8B, HotPotQA. Seconds per query. The in-context learning row is a no-cache baseline, not RAG.
  quote: "The results demonstrate that CAG dramatically reduces generation time, particularly as the reference text length increases."
  where: Table 3 and Figure 2 (p.3-4)
- CAG's generation time grows with corpus size (0.85 s to 2.26 s). Sparse RAG stays near-flat, and CAG is not faster than sparse RAG. The paper says CAG is more efficient than dense RAG only.
  number: CAG 0.8512 to 2.2631 s. Sparse top-3 0.7406 to 0.6667 s. Dense top-3 retrieval plus generation is about 1.49 s (small) and 1.35 s (large).
  setup: same as above
  quote: "However, CAG remains more efficient than dense RAG, as it avoids retrieval overhead while maintaining comparable or superior response times."
  where: Section 3.3
- Sparse RAG often beat dense RAG. The authors read this as a sign the datasets are easy, not as a point about retrieval methods.
  number: HotPotQA small top-1: sparse 0.6788 vs dense 0.7164, so dense wins at k=1 there. SQuAD small top-1: sparse 0.7214 vs dense 0.6216. SQuAD large top-1: 0.7254 vs 0.6070.
  setup: same as Table 2
  quote: "Additionally, the fact that sparse RAG outperforms dense RAG suggests that the datasets may not be sufficiently challenging, allowing traditional sparse retrieval to effectively capture most relevant information without requiring deeper semantic retrieval."
  where: Section 3.3
- Design premise: modern long-context models have an effective context well below their nominal 128K, and that range covers many knowledge bases.
  number: 128K trained length. Effective length 32K (8B) and 64K (70B).
  setup: Llama 3.1, citing RULER (Hsieh 2024). The figures are quoted from the literature, not measured here.
  quote: "Llama 3.1 [1] was trained with a 128K context length, and its effective context length is 32K in Llama 3.1 8B and 64K in Llama 3.1 70B [3]."
  where: Section 1 (p.1)
- Method in three phases: preload documents and encode them once into a KV cache; load the cache with the query at inference; reset by truncating the appended query tokens.
  number: none
  setup: The one-time cost of encoding is independent of query count. The cache grows append-only, so reset is truncation.
  quote: "As the KV cache grows in an append-only manner with new tokens q = (t1, t2, . . . , tk ) sequentially appended, resetting involves truncating these new tokens."
  where: Section 2
- Proposed hybrid: preload a foundation context and retrieve only for edge cases. Stated as future potential, with no experiment.
  number: none
  quote: "a system could preload a foundation context and use retrieval only to augment edge cases or highly specific queries."
  where: Section 4

Test sets (Table 1): HotPotQA small/medium/large = 16/32/64 docs, 21k/43k/85k tokens, 1,392/1,056/1,344 QA pairs. SQuAD small/medium/large = 3/4/7 docs, 21k/32k/50k tokens, 500 QA pairs each.

LIMITS
- Authors concede: "this approach becomes impractical for significantly larger datasets." They suggest the limit will ease as context windows grow. Suited to small internal KBs, FAQs and call centres.
- Largest corpus tested is 85k tokens, which exceeds the 32K effective length they cite for Llama 3.1 8B. The paper does not discuss this.
- One model (Llama 3.1 8B), two QA benchmarks, one metric (BERTScore, an embedding-similarity score that is weak at judging factual correctness). No exact-match, F1 or human or LLM judge. No variance or significance tests.
- RAG baselines are plain LlamaIndex top-k. No reranking, chunking sweeps, hybrid retrieval or query rewriting. The authors themselves note the datasets are too easy for dense retrieval to show its strengths.
- The in-context learning baseline is a strawman for latency, since it recomputes the KV cache each query. Nothing is said about KV cache memory cost, cache size on disk, or updating the corpus (a change means re-encoding).
- No cost, throughput or concurrency measurements. Latency is only shown for HotPotQA, not SQuAD.
- The title ("Don't Do RAG") overstates the evidence. The data supports CAG on small, static, bounded corpora, and the margin disappears at 85k tokens on HotPotQA.
- Dated: the models are Llama 3.1 era. Newer long-context models and prompt caching APIs were not tested.

BUILDS ON: Lewis et al. 2020 (RAG); Gao et al. 2023 (RAG survey); Li, Li et al. 2024 (RAG or long-context LLMs, hybrid approach, EMNLP Industry); Leng et al. 2024 (Long Context RAG Performance); Lu et al. 2024 (TurboRAG, precomputed KV caches for chunked text, needs position-ID rearrangement); Pope et al. 2023 (efficiently scaling transformer inference, KV cache); Hsieh et al. 2024 (RULER); Li, Zhang et al. 2024 (long-context LLMs struggle with long in-context learning); Dubey et al. 2024 (Llama 3); Rajpurkar 2016 (SQuAD); Yang 2018 (HotpotQA); Zhang et al. (BERTScore).

CODE: none in the paper. Code is released at https://github.com/hhhuang/CAG (not read).

FIGURES
- Fig 1 (p.2): RAG vs CAG workflow. The IR model sits in the inference path for RAG. For CAG, knowledge is preloaded offline into a cache and only the query is processed at inference. Fastest way to see the architecture difference.
- Fig 2 (p.4): stacked bars of retrieval vs generation time on HotPotQA small/medium/large. Same data as Table 3. I did not view the images, only the caption text.

PROBLEMS: No embedded instructions found. The text has many hyphenation and spacing artifacts from extraction (for example "Austra lia"), and the fontTools warnings are noise. The PDF ends with two stray arXiv "figure available" placeholders (acm logo, sample-franklin), which are template leftovers. Table 2 is flattened, but its columns align as HotPotQA then SQuAD. Where a CAG row carries one value per column, I read it as HotPotQA first, SQuAD second.
